opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, because I think people tend to frame AI and energy as a story about how much power data centers are going to need. That's real. But the deeper shift is about *where* the value of energy gets created.

Historically, if you had cheap energy in a remote place, say a lot of solar in a desert, stranded natural gas, or a big hydro resource far from any city, you had a hard problem. You had to build transmission lines, pipelines, or LNG terminals and ship that energy to where people and factories were. That's expensive, slow, politically difficult, and you lose a lot along the way.

AI changes that a bit, because intelligence is incredibly cheap to move. You can turn energy into computation wherever the energy is, and then send the results around the world over fiber at almost no cost. In some sense, a data center is a way of converting electrons into something you can ship at the speed of light. So instead of moving the energy to the people, you can move the compute to the energy and then move the intelligence to the people.

I don't want to overstate it. You still need power for homes, for manufacturing, for transportation, and none of that goes away. And building these huge clusters brings its own hard problems: permitting, grid interconnection, cooling, supply chains for chips and transformers. But I think it means the map of where energy is valuable could look quite different over the next decade or two. Places with abundant, cheap, clean power that were never economically central could become really important.

The other side is that AI should help with the energy problem itself: better materials, better grid management, maybe help on fusion and next-generation fission, better batteries. If we get that right, the long-term picture I'm excited about is that the cost of intelligence and the cost of energy both come way down together. Those two things are pretty much the fundamental inputs to everything else we want to do.

r001.rationale: It explains that energy can be converted into computation where it is available, then the resulting intelligence can be sent around the world over fiber far more easily than moving the energy itself.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I think about this a lot, because energy might be the thing that ends up mattering most in all of this. The weird thing about energy is that it's abundant in the wrong places. There's incredible solar in deserts where nobody lives, and huge demand in cities where there's no room for it. And historically moving it has been really hard. Transmission lines take a decade to permit, you lose a lot over distance, and the whole grid is this fragile, balanced thing that nobody fully understands.

What I think AI does is a couple of things. The first, which is a little counterintuitive, is that it makes the problem bigger before it makes it smaller. The demand for compute is enormous, and compute is basically energy in a different form. So we're going to need a lot more electricity, and we're going to need it in a lot of new places.

But the second thing is that AI changes what you move. If you have a data center next to a solar field in a place where no one would ever build a city, you don't have to move the electrons. You move the intelligence instead, over a fiber optic cable, and that's almost free compared to a transmission line. So in a sense, compute becomes a way to export energy. I think that's going to reshape where things get built.

And then the third piece is that the grid itself gets a lot smarter. Right now we overbuild everything because we can't predict demand well, and we can't coordinate millions of devices in real time. I think AI gets pretty good at that, and that means you can run the system much closer to the edge, with more renewables and less waste.

So I'd say the challenge doesn't go away, but it changes shape. The bottleneck really becomes how fast we can build, which is a question about permitting and will more than technology. That's the part I worry about.

r001.rationale: The candidate says intelligence can be moved over fiber optic cable instead of transmitting electrons over long-distance power lines, describing that as almost free by comparison.

astra-6.text:
I think AI can help us get much better at managing the grid—predicting demand, figuring out where we need more capacity, and coordinating generation and storage. But moving energy is still a physical challenge. You have to build transmission lines, and that takes time.

One interesting thing about AI is that you can move some of the demand instead. For workloads that are flexible about location and timing, you can put the compute near abundant energy and send the results around the world. Moving information is much easier than moving electricity.

So I think you’ll see both: AI helping us use energy infrastructure more efficiently, and energy availability shaping where we build AI infrastructure.

r001.rationale: The response says flexible compute can be placed near abundant energy and its results sent around the world, while moving information is easier than moving electricity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI can help us operate the grid more efficiently—forecasting demand, matching it to supply, figuring out where storage or new transmission would have the biggest impact. But moving energy is still a physical problem. You have to build things, and software doesn’t make those constraints disappear.

The interesting question is how much we can move the computation instead. If you have abundant energy somewhere, you can put a data center there and send the results around the world. That won’t work for every workload, and it doesn’t solve the broader transmission problem, but it gives you another way to connect energy supply with demand.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the physical constraints of transmitting energy with placing a data center where energy is abundant and sending its results around the world.
